records.licence: unknown (no reuse licence stated on the list landing page; Linux Foundation site terms of use apply)
records.finding: Licence identity is a stable short string, not prose: every listed licence and exception has a short identifier, a full name, canonical licence text and a permanent URL, identifiers are never repurposed and are deprecated instead, and the list stays deliberately neutral by recording OSI approval and FSF free status as two separate flag columns rather than one verdict. The operational rule is that a dependency record carries an identifier, and any judgement about that identifier is made once, centrally, against the identifier.
records.applicability_limits: A naming registry only. It confers no permission, states no obligations, ranks nothing and says nothing about whether a combination is lawful; it also cannot describe a licence that is not on the list except through a LicenseRef.
records.counter_evidence: The deliberate neutrality means the list will happily give an identifier to a licence that is neither open source nor safe to depend on, so an allowlist keyed on identifiers still needs a separate policy layer.

records.licence: Community Specification License 1.0 and CC BY 3.0 Unported
records.finding: Real licensing is compound and the grammar says so: AND means every listed licence must be complied with at once, OR means the recipient chooses one, WITH attaches a named exception, the plus suffix means that version or later, LicenseRef covers anything off the list, and precedence runs plus, WITH, AND, OR with parentheses overriding. The decision rule this yields is that an OR expression is a choice a project must actually record having made, and an AND expression is a set of obligations that all bite.
records.applicability_limits: Syntax, not semantics. The grammar cannot tell you whether an AND combination is lawful, and a tool that emits a well-formed expression has still only reported what a file claims about itself.
records.counter_evidence: The annex read here does not cover NOASSERTION and NONE, which is where most real scan output lands, so the tidy grammar understates how much of a dependency tree resolves to nothing usable.

records.source: Open Source Initiative, The Open Source Definition
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 (site content, attribution to Opensource.org)
records.finding: The ten criteria define open source by what a licence may not restrict rather than by what it must require: no restriction on redistribution or sale, source in preferred form, derived works permitted under the same terms, no discrimination against persons or fields of endeavour, rights travelling automatically with the code, and no product, technology or interface specificity. A licence that limits the field of use, however reasonable the limit sounds, is not open source under this definition and the venture should treat it as proprietary.
records.applicability_limits: A definition of licence eligibility, not a compatibility rule and not a risk rating. It has been stable since 2007 and says nothing about source-available, ethical-source or business-source licences that have appeared since.
records.counter_evidence: OSI approval and safety are different axes: a licence can satisfy all ten criteria and still be drafted badly enough that Blue Oak rates it lead, and conversely a non-approved licence may be trivially safe to use.

records.source: Free Software Foundation, License Compatibility and Relicensing
records.licence: CC BY-ND 4.0 (no derivatives, so paraphrase the principle and never adapt the text)
records.finding: Compatibility means you can merge the code and still comply with every licence at once, and it is directional: lax licences absorb into anything, copyleft licences are unavoidably incompatible with each other unless one of them carries an explicit compatibility provision. Two named consequences that a routing rule must encode are that GPLv2 and GPLv3 do not combine, and that the Apache 2.0 patent terms are incompatible with GPLv2 while GPLv3 was written to accept them.
records.applicability_limits: The position of one advocacy organisation, stated as doctrine rather than tested in court, and it addresses combination of source into one program. It does not settle where a program boundary lies for a service, a container image or a plug-in.
records.counter_evidence: The FSF frames the same facts as an argument for choosing GPLv3-or-later, whereas the ASF policy reads the identical incompatibility as a reason to exclude the GPL family entirely; the facts agree and the recommended action does not.

records.source: GNU Affero General Public License version 3, OSI-hosted text
records.version_or_commit: AGPL-3.0, approved 2008-03-03; page licence per opensource.org footer
records.licence: CC BY 4.0 for the OSI page; the licence text itself is copyright FSF, verbatim copying permitted, modification not permitted
records.finding: Section 13 moves the trigger from distribution to interaction: a modified version that users reach remotely over a network must offer those users the corresponding source of that version from a network server at no charge, and the licence explicitly permits combination with GPLv3 work with each part keeping its own terms. For a venture whose product is a hosted service this is the one copyleft term that bites without anything ever being shipped, so AGPL dependencies need a decision before they enter, not at release.
records.applicability_limits: The obligation attaches to a modified version made available to remote users; the licence text alone does not resolve what counts as modification, what counts as the same program when the AGPL code sits behind an internal service boundary, or how the offer must be surfaced.
records.counter_evidence: Read narrowly, an unmodified AGPL component run as a back end triggers nothing extra, which is why some teams treat AGPL as usable and others ban it outright; the disagreement is about the modification boundary, not about the text.

records.source: Apache Software Foundation, ASF third-party licence policy
records.version_or_commit: unknown (no revision or last-modified date shown on the page)
records.finding: The reusable shape is a standing three-bucket verdict decided once by people and then applied mechanically by everyone else: category A may be included freely with attribution, category B may be included in binary form only in convenience distributions and never in a source release, and category X may not be distributed at all. GPL and AGPL sit in X because they impose terms on the larger work, weak copyleft such as MPL, EPL and CDDL sits in B, and one narrow exception, GPLv2 with the Classpath exception, is carved out explicitly rather than by case-by-case judgement.
records.applicability_limits: This is a policy tuned to one distributor's promise, that everything it releases stays permissively licensed. It reasons about source and binary releases, so it does not directly answer questions about a hosted service, an internal tool or a build-time-only dependency.
records.counter_evidence: The blanket exclusion of GPL is stricter than the law requires for a venture that never distributes the combined work, so copying the categories without copying the reason produces a rule that blocks safe dependencies while saying nothing about the network trigger that actually matters.

records.source: Blue Oak Council Permissive License List
records.licence: unknown (no reuse licence stated on the list page; the list is also published as JSON and as an npm package)
records.finding: Permissive is not one bucket, it is a quality gradient, and the gradient is publishable as machine-readable data: gold for licences that address patents explicitly, use robust drafting and ask only for simple notice, silver for strong drafting missing patent terms or asking more than notice, bronze for missing but non-essential elements or awkward extra restrictions, lead for missing essential elements or burdensome and informally worded terms. The rule this supports is that the rating is a tiebreak for choosing an outbound licence and for triaging inbound risk, never a permission.
records.applicability_limits: The ratings are the collective judgement of the council's lawyers, not a measurement or a legal opinion for any specific use, and the list covers permissive licences only, so it is silent on every copyleft question.
records.counter_evidence: A licence can be OSI approved and rated lead, so this axis and the Open Source Definition axis will sometimes point in opposite directions for the same licence.

records.source: REUSE Specification, Free Software Foundation Europe
records.finding: Licensing becomes checkable when it is declared per file rather than inferred per repository: every covered file carries SPDX-FileCopyrightText and SPDX-License-Identifier in a comment header, files that cannot carry comments get a sibling .license file, every licence referenced has its full text in LICENSES/ named by SPDX identifier, and bulk cases are declared in REUSE.toml by glob with defined precedence. A lint tool then turns the whole question into a pass or fail in CI, which is what makes it enforceable by a cold agent.
records.applicability_limits: It proves declarations are present and internally consistent, nothing more. A conformant repository can still declare the wrong licence, and the specification says nothing about whether the declared combination is compatible.
records.counter_evidence: The per-file discipline is real overhead on small repositories, and repository-level detection tools deliberately guess instead, which is why most projects in the wild are not conformant.

records.licence: copyright the Linux Foundation and its contributors; verbatim copying and distribution permitted, modification not permitted
records.finding: Inbound contribution rights can be handled by certification rather than by contract: the contributor asserts that they wrote the change and may submit it, or that it derives from work they are entitled to submit under a compatible open source licence, or that someone who so certified passed it to them unmodified, and they accept that the record is public and permanent. The obligation is discharged by one sign-off line per commit, which a hook can check, so the process cost is near zero and the evidence is in the history.
records.applicability_limits: The DCO is an assertion by the contributor, not a grant of rights to the project, and it presumes the project already has an inbound licence that the contribution comes under. It gives no patent grant and no warranty, and it does not help with contributions of code the contributor was wrong about.
records.counter_evidence: Projects that need to relicense later, or that want explicit patent and moral-rights positions, use a contributor licence agreement instead; no source read at this cutoff compares the two on outcomes, so the choice rests on assertion rather than evidence.

records.licence: Apache-2.0 for the code, CC-BY-4.0 for the reference licence datasets, bundled third-party components under their own terms including LGPL and GPL
records.finding: Licence detection works by full text comparison against a curated database of licence texts rather than by regular-expression matching on headers, and it scans copyrights, package manifests and declared dependencies in the same pass, which is what lets a build emit an inventory instead of a guess. The practical rule is that the scanner produces the inventory and a human produces the verdict.
records.applicability_limits: The project claims the most accurate detection engine but publishes no accuracy figure on the page read here, and no statement was found disclaiming legal advice, so the accuracy claim is a vendor claim. Detection also cannot see licence terms that exist only in a separate agreement or in a file the scan does not cover.
records.counter_evidence: Repository-level detectors used by hosting platforms disagree with file-level scans routinely, and a scan of a project that follows REUSE is answering a much easier question than a scan of one that does not, so measured accuracy is not portable between codebases.

records.licence: CC BY 4.0 for the specification documents, CC0 for the reference material
records.finding: The standard certifies a process, not an artefact, and it is deliberately minimal: name the places in the lifecycle where compliance decisions happen, assign the roles and responsibilities that make those decisions, and show the arrangement is sustainable rather than a one-off audit. Conformance can be self-declared against a published checklist or attested by a third party, and the two routes are treated as the same standard rather than two tiers of truth.
records.applicability_limits: Written for organisations with staff to assign roles to; a one-person venture can satisfy the letter trivially and learn nothing. It says nothing about which licences to accept and nothing about how to resolve a specific compatibility question.
records.counter_evidence: Self-certification against your own checklist is exactly the failure mode a standard is supposed to prevent, and no source read here measures whether conformant organisations have fewer licence incidents.

records.version_or_commit: unknown (no version or revision date shown; GitHub-maintained site)
records.finding: Absence of a licence is not permission, it is exclusive copyright by default, and platform mechanics do not change that: hosting terms may let anyone view and fork a public repository while granting no right to use, modify or redistribute the code. The only routes out are to ask the owner to add a licence, to find an alternative, or to negotiate a private licence, so an unlicensed dependency is a blocking finding rather than an unknown to be filled in later.
records.applicability_limits: Guidance written by a hosting platform for the general case, not legal advice and not jurisdiction-specific; it also addresses public repositories on that platform and does not cover code received privately or under a separate agreement.

records.source: UK GDPR Article 13, information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
records.version_or_commit: revised text showing amendments up to 2026-08-02, including Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 changes in force from 2026-02-05
records.licence: Open Government Licence v3.0, with material reused from EUR-Lex under Commission Decision 2011/833/EU
records.finding: A privacy notice is a fixed checklist due at the moment of collection, not a document written when convenient: controller identity and contact, any data protection officer, purposes and lawful basis, the legitimate interests relied on where that is the basis, categories of recipient, third-country transfers and safeguards, retention period or the criteria for it, the access, rectification, erasure and restriction rights, withdrawal of consent, and the automated decision-making position. The revised UK text now also names two distinct complaint routes that must be told to the subject, to the controller under section 164A and to the Commissioner under section 165.
records.applicability_limits: Statutory duty in the UK only, and it states what must be said, not how to say it, at what reading level or in what format. It is silent on the harder questions of whether the chosen lawful basis is correct and whether the processing itself is fair.

records.source: The Data Protection (Charges and Information) Regulations 2018
records.version_or_commit: SI 2018 No. 480, original text as made
records.finding: There is a statutory duty on data controllers to pay a charge to the Information Commissioner and to supply information, with the amount set by regulation, special handling for partnerships and for school governing bodies, and a schedule of exempt processing. For a venture the routing consequence is binary and cheap to check: before any personal data is processed, run the registration self-assessment and either pay or record which schedule exemption applies, because this is a duty that exists independently of how good the privacy notice is.
records.applicability_limits: The version read is the text as originally made, so the tier amounts stated in it may have been uprated since and must be checked against the current fee before relying on a number. Only the table of contents and structure were retrieved at this access, not the tier figures.

records.source: European Commission, summary of the Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847)
records.version_or_commit: Regulation (EU) 2024/2847; entry into force 2024-12-10, conformity assessment bodies from 2026-06-11, reporting obligations from 2026-09-11, full application from 2027-12-11
records.licence: unknown (no reuse notice shown on the page; Commission Decision 2011/833/EU typically applies to Commission documents)
records.finding: The regulator's line is drawn at commercial activity, not at price: free and open-source software published outside a commercial activity is out of scope, but the same software made available on the market in the course of a commercial activity is in, and a manufacturer is anyone who markets a product with digital elements under their own name whether paid, monetised or free. A separate lighter category, the open-source software steward, carries a duty to keep a documented cybersecurity policy and to handle vulnerability reports but attracts no penalties.
records.applicability_limits: EU market scope, so it reaches a UK venture only through what it places on that market, and this is the Commission's own summary rather than the operative text of the Regulation, which was not retrieved at this access. It sets obligations without telling a very small manufacturer what proportionate evidence looks like.
records.counter_evidence: The boundary between publishing open source and making it available in the course of a commercial activity is the contested part, and the summary asserts the line without resolving the cases that matter, such as a maintainer with sponsorship or a hosted version of their own project.

records.source: United States Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence report
records.version_or_commit: Part 1 Digital Replicas 2024-07-31 final; Part 2 Copyrightability 2025-01-29 final; Part 3 Generative AI Training 2025-05-09 pre-publication, final version expected without substantive change
records.finding: The question of who owns machine-generated output is being answered by a national copyright authority in staged public reports rather than settled, and the staging itself is the signal: copyrightability and training data are separate inquiries with separate conclusions. A venture shipping agent-written code should therefore treat authorship and provenance as an open position to record, not a solved one to assume.
records.applicability_limits: United States law and the position of one office, not binding in the UK and not a court ruling. The hub page read here does not state the Office's conclusions on the human-contribution threshold, so no threshold should be quoted from this record; the underlying part reports were not read at this cutoff.
records.counter_evidence: No equivalent UK determination was located at this cutoff, so the UK position on agent-written code is genuinely unresolved rather than merely unread.
